why_it_matters: It connects abstract entanglement geometry to operational metrological resource value for distributed quantum sensing.
detailed_summary: The paper proves that Entanglement Distance from the Fubini-Study metric is mathematically identical to Meyer-Wallach and Scott multipartite entanglement measures for arbitrary finite-dimensional pure states. It derives the measure as the trace of the Fubini-Study metric tensor over the local observable subalgebra. The result gives an operational interpretation: global pure-state entanglement is proportional to the total Quantum Fisher Information available for local unitary estimation.
main_result: The main result is an exact equivalence between geometric entanglement distance, linear-entropy entanglement measures, and total local-estimation QFI.
application_angle: The framework helps identify entangled states that are practically useful for distributed quantum sensing and Heisenberg-limited estimation.

title: An exchange-assisted entangling gate between 87Rb and 171Yb Rydberg atoms
abstract: Neutral-atom tweezer arrays support scalable quantum information processing. Dual-species $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$--$^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ arrays combine long-lived ytterbium nuclear-spin data qubits with fast, species-selective rubidium ancilla control and readout. However, realizing interspecies gates without inducing destructive Stark mixing in divalent atoms remains an outstanding problem. Here, we identify an optically accessible $S{+}S\leftrightarrow P{+}P$ Förster resonance at zero electric field, providing strong dipole-dipole exchange at array pitch. Using a shaped optical pulse under finite control response, we demonstrate a $0.36\,μ\mathrm{s}$ exchange-assisted controlled-$Z$ gate with an intrinsic fidelity of $99.91\%$, remaining above $99.85\%$ under bounded perturbations. We also identify an auxiliary repulsive van der Waals channel, providing a comprehensive toolbox for hybrid quantum processors.
one_liner: A proposed Rb-Yb Rydberg gate uses a zero-field Förster exchange channel to realize fast high-fidelity interspecies CZ operation.
why_it_matters: It addresses a key missing primitive for dual-species neutral-atom processors with Yb data qubits and Rb ancilla control.
detailed_summary: The work identifies an optically accessible S+S to P+P Förster resonance between 87Rb and 171Yb Rydberg atoms at zero electric field. This exchange channel provides strong dipole-dipole coupling at tweezer-array pitch while avoiding destructive Stark mixing in divalent Yb. With a shaped optical pulse and finite control response included, the authors report a 0.36 us exchange-assisted CZ gate with 99.91% intrinsic fidelity and robustness above 99.85% under bounded perturbations.
main_result: The paper demonstrates a design for a 0.36 us interspecies Rydberg CZ gate with 99.91% intrinsic fidelity.
application_angle: Fast species-selective interconnects could improve architectures that combine long-lived Yb memory qubits with Rb ancilla operations and readout.

title: Strong Converse for Quantum Capacity via a Fully Quantum Blowing-Up Lemma
abstract: We prove an exponential strong converse for quantum communication through every finite-dimensional memoryless channel: at any fixed rate above the quantum capacity, the entanglement-transmission fidelity of every code decays exponentially with the number of channel uses. The proof has two main ingredients. First, a fully quantum blowing-up lemma converts a low-fidelity code into a high-fidelity code, with a loss in the number of transmitted qubits controlled by the projective tensor norm of the orthogonal projection on the image of the Stinespring dilation of the channel across the receiver--environment bipartition. Second, a low-degree polynomial construction approximates the tensor power of this projector with exponential accuracy while controlling its projective norm, providing the approximation needed for the blowing-up argument.
one_liner: Proves an exponential strong converse for quantum capacity of all finite-dimensional memoryless quantum channels.
why_it_matters: It sharpens capacity as a true operational threshold: above it, quantum communication fidelity must vanish exponentially with blocklength.
detailed_summary: The paper proves that any code communicating above the quantum capacity of a finite-dimensional memoryless channel has entanglement-transmission fidelity decaying exponentially in the number of channel uses. The proof introduces a fully quantum blowing-up lemma and controls the rate loss through a projective tensor norm tied to the channel Stinespring image. A low-degree polynomial approximation to tensor powers of the relevant projector supplies the exponential accuracy needed for the argument.
main_result: An exponential strong converse is established for quantum communication through every finite-dimensional memoryless channel.
application_angle: This gives rigorous performance limits for quantum network links and channel-coding benchmarks beyond asymptotic achievability statements.

title: SI-Traceable Calibration and Performance Benchmarking of a Terahertz Photomixer Transmitter-Receiver System Using a Rydberg Atomic Sensor
abstract: Accurate calibration of electromagnetic field strength in the terahertz (THz) frequency regime remains challenging due to the limited availability of SI-traceable field sensors. Here we demonstrate SI-traceable calibration and performance benchmarking of a commercial photomixer-based THz transmitter-receiver system operating near 204 GHz using Rydberg electric-field sensing in a thermal atomic vapor. The THz electric field is extracted from the Autler-Townes (AT) effect of the cesium $17D_{5/2}\rightarrow18P_{3/2}$ Rydberg transition. We measure the strength of AT-split lines as a function of THz detuning from resonance to find the on-resonant Rabi frequency, which, together with atomic transition dipole moments and fundamental constants, yields the THz electric field. The atomically measured field calibrates the photomixer transmitter field and power, while simultaneous measurements with a commercial InGaAs photomixer receiver calibrate the receiver's current-to-field responsivity and convert its current-noise floor into an absolute noise-equivalent THz electric-field sensitivity. Our study demonstrates that Rydberg atomic sensors provide a practical method for SI-traceable calibration and benchmarking of THz transmitter and receiver systems, and for the establishment of a quantitative link between state-of-the-art and absolute atom-based THz sensors.
one_liner: Uses cesium Rydberg atoms to SI-calibrate a 204 GHz photomixer THz transmitter-receiver system.
why_it_matters: It links commercial THz photomixer hardware to absolute atom-based field standards, improving traceable benchmarking of THz systems.
detailed_summary: The work calibrates a commercial photomixer-based transmitter-receiver system near 204 GHz using Rydberg electric-field sensing in thermal cesium vapor. THz field strength is extracted from Autler-Townes splitting on the Cs 17D5/2 to 18P3/2 transition, using known dipole moments and constants to obtain an SI-traceable field. Simultaneous InGaAs photomixer receiver measurements convert current response and noise into absolute field responsivity and noise-equivalent THz sensitivity.
main_result: The authors demonstrate SI-traceable calibration of transmitter field, power, receiver responsivity, and THz electric-field sensitivity near 204 GHz.
application_angle: The method offers a practical calibration route for THz communications, spectroscopy, metrology, and hardware qualification.

title: EFI Pairs Without One-Way Puzzles: Oracle Separations from Communication Complexity
abstract: EFI pairs (Brakerski, Canetti, and Qian, ITCS 2023) and one-way puzzles (Khurana and Tomer, STOC 2024) are the leading candidates for the minimal assumption of quantum cryptography. The first are efficiently preparable quantum states, statistically far yet computationally indistinguishable; the second are classical puzzles, easy to sample and hard to solve. One-way puzzles imply EFI pairs, and whether the converse holds is open. We construct a single classical oracle relative to which one-way puzzles do not exist, even with an unbounded verifier, while an EFI pair survives every distinguisher that queries the oracle classically throughout and holds advice about it, making its one superposition query at the end. The oracle answers every question about the output probabilities of quantum samplers, which removes the puzzles, and hides a Haar-random half-dimensional subspace. To prove security we reduce it to communication complexity. An adversary whose knowledge of the subspace arrives as classical query answers can be simulated inside a two-party protocol against the party holding it, so it does no better than the best classical protocol for Vector-in-Subspace (Klartag and Regev, STOC 2011), whatever the oracle computes. That argument does not cover the superposition query, which we bound instead using tools from random matrix theory. The same attack gives a classical simulation of any quantum party in a classical-message protocol with no entanglement shared in advance, so relative to the oracle there is no proof of quantumness either. Quantum polynomial time therefore offers no advantage on any task with classical inputs and outputs, while the two quantum states stay indistinguishable. We state conjectures on removing the restriction on superposition queries.
one_liner: Builds an oracle world where EFI quantum state pairs exist but one-way puzzles do not.
why_it_matters: It separates candidate minimal assumptions for quantum cryptography and clarifies what EFI pairs can imply in black-box settings.
detailed_summary: The paper constructs a classical oracle that eliminates one-way puzzles, even with an unbounded verifier, while preserving an EFI pair against a restricted class of quantum distinguishers. The oracle exposes output probabilities of quantum samplers but hides a Haar-random half-dimensional subspace. Security is reduced to communication complexity for Vector-in-Subspace, with the remaining superposition-query component bounded using random matrix theory.
main_result: An oracle separation shows EFI pairs need not imply one-way puzzles under the stated query restrictions.
application_angle: The result refines the assumption landscape behind quantum cryptographic primitives and proofs of quantumness.

title: The generalised semi-Clifford conjecture is false
abstract: The Clifford hierarchy is a nested sequence of sets of quantum gates that can be fault-tolerantly performed using gate teleportation within standard quantum error correction schemes. The importance of these gates has motivated numerous studies of their structure. Zeng-Chen-Chuang conjectured in 2007 that all hierarchy gates are generalised semi-Clifford, i.e. take the form $C_1 ΠD C_2$ for Clifford gates $C_1, C_2$, a permutation gate $Π$, and a diagonal gate $D$; Beigi-Shor proved in 2008 that this holds for all third-level gates. We construct a five-qubit gate that is in the fifth level of the Clifford hierarchy but is not generalised semi-Clifford. Rather than simply present and verify our counterexample to the generalised semi-Clifford conjecture, we show how its form can be deduced. Our counterexample also demonstrates that the Clifford hierarchy is not closed under inverses.
one_liner: Constructs a five-qubit Clifford-hierarchy gate that disproves the generalized semi-Clifford conjecture.
why_it_matters: It changes structural expectations for fault-tolerant gate sets and shows the Clifford hierarchy is richer than assumed.
detailed_summary: The paper gives a five-qubit gate in the fifth level of the Clifford hierarchy that cannot be written as a generalized semi-Clifford gate of the form C1 Pi D C2. It also explains how the counterexample can be derived rather than merely verified. The construction further shows that the Clifford hierarchy is not closed under inverses.
main_result: A concrete fifth-level five-qubit counterexample disproves the generalized semi-Clifford conjecture.
application_angle: The finding affects compilation, teleportation-based fault tolerance, and classification of implementable non-Clifford resources.

title: A Chip-scale Space-time Multiplexed Gaussian Boson Sampling Processor Beyond 10,000 Photons
abstract: Gaussian boson sampling (GBS) has emerged as a leading photonic paradigmfor demonstrating quantum computational advantage. Nevertheless, state-ofthe-art GBS setups face practical barriers including stringent optical alignment, phase instability, and limited programmability, which impede scalable engineering deployment. The chip-scale space-time multiplexed architecturepromises to resolve these constraints, yet it strongly demands wafer-scale chipcapabilities to simultaneously satisfy stringent requirements on low loss, highprecision and high-speed modulation. Here we report the first chip-scale spacetime multiplexed GBS system, monolithically integrating high-speed electrooptic modulators, on-chip delay lines, and a time-space multiplexed interferometric network on a thin-film lithium niobate chip, operating at a 4-GHz clockrate with detection events of up to 11,059 photons within 1 millisecond. Beyond benchmarking quantum advantage, we further reconfigure the photonichardware into a GBS-powered world model for modelling physical dynamics,which achieves lower prediction error with fewer trainable readout parameters compared with a classical echo state network (ESN) baseline. Our resultsvalidate the feasibility of our endeavor towards scalable photonic quantumhardware, and pave the way for the versatile programmable applications offuture GBS quantum systems.
one_liner: Demonstrates a thin-film lithium niobate GBS processor exceeding 10,000 detected photons in 1 ms.
why_it_matters: It is a major chip-scale photonic hardware step, combining high-speed modulation, delay lines, and programmable interferometry on one platform.
detailed_summary: The authors report a chip-scale space-time multiplexed Gaussian boson sampling processor on thin-film lithium niobate. The system monolithically integrates high-speed electro-optic modulators, on-chip delay lines, and a time-space multiplexed interferometric network, operating at a 4 GHz clock rate. It records detection events up to 11,059 photons within 1 ms and is reconfigured as a GBS-powered world model for physical-dynamics prediction.
platform_or_system: thin-film lithium niobate photonic GBS chip
main_result: The processor achieves up to 11,059 detected photons in 1 ms and outperforms a classical ESN baseline in a reconfigured modeling task.
application_angle: The architecture points toward scalable programmable photonic processors for quantum advantage tests and application-oriented optical computing.

title: Quantifying Symmetry Breaking
abstract: Quantifying properties of quantum states through the limits of their manipulation is a central goal of quantum resource theories. For symmetry breaking, the quantum geometric tensor governs asymptotic pure-state conversion, but a complete characterization for general mixed states has remained elusive. Here we fully resolve this problem for finite-dimensional systems under compact Lie group symmetries in the i.i.d. asymptotic regime. Specifically, we establish a single-letter formula for the optimal conversion rate between arbitrary states, with vanishing trace-distance error, in the resource theory of asymmetry. The rate is determined by a one-parameter family of quantum Fisher information (QFI) matrices that interpolates between the symmetric- and right-logarithmic-derivative QFIs. No state-independent finite subset of this family suffices in general, even for $U(1)$ symmetry, revealing a qualitative distinction from pure-state conversion. Our formula further yields an exact formula for pure-state distillation rates in terms of the generalized quantum geometric tensor, characterizes asymptotically reversible interconversion, and identifies bound asymmetry for quantum clocks. Complementarity among different members of the QFI family also uncovers an activation mechanism for quantum clocks. Our proof relies on two developments of independent interest. First, we extend quantum local asymptotic normality to unitary models with arbitrary rank and spectral degeneracy. Second, we characterize convertibility between quantum Gaussian shift models in terms of the same one-parameter family of QFIs. Together, these results provide an operational characterization of symmetry breaking for general quantum states in the i.i.d. asymptotic regime and reveal how distinct QFI constraints give rise to irreversibility and activation.
one_liner: Gives a full asymptotic resource-theory formula for symmetry breaking in finite-dimensional mixed quantum states.
why_it_matters: It connects quantum Fisher information families to operational limits for clocks, asymmetry conversion, and metrological resources.
detailed_summary: The paper resolves asymptotic i.i.d. conversion rates for arbitrary finite-dimensional states under compact Lie group symmetries. The optimal rate is given by a one-parameter family of quantum Fisher information matrices interpolating between symmetric- and right-logarithmic-derivative QFIs. The results identify irreversibility, bound asymmetry for quantum clocks, and activation mechanisms arising from complementarity among QFI constraints.
main_result: A single-letter formula is derived for optimal mixed-state asymmetry conversion rates with vanishing trace-distance error.
application_angle: The framework gives operational limits for quantum clocks, timing references, and sensing resources based on symmetry breaking.

title: Log-depth entanglement transition in hypercube Gaussian boson sampling
abstract: We study an entanglement transition at logarithmic depth in random hypercube linear optical networks. Starting from an initial Gaussian state with all modes squeezed, we prove that random hypercube linear optical networks on $n$ modes generate ensemble-averaged subsystem entanglement within a constant factor of its maximum in all subsystems at circuit depth $Θ(\log n)$. Below depth $\log_2n$, there is an extensive subsystem with no entanglement. The entanglement generation in logarithmic depth can be compared to recent progress towards $O(\log n)$ depth average-case sampling hardness for Gaussian boson sampling in a hypercube network.
one_liner: Shows logarithmic-depth random hypercube linear optics can generate near-maximal averaged entanglement in Gaussian boson sampling.
why_it_matters: Connects photonic network depth, entanglement growth, and sampling-hardness architecture requirements for scalable Gaussian boson sampling.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes random hypercube linear-optical circuits on n squeezed modes and proves an entanglement transition at depth Theta(log n). Above this depth, ensemble-averaged subsystem entanglement reaches within a constant factor of its maximum for all subsystems, while below log2 n an extensive subsystem remains unentangled. The result gives a hardware-relevant depth scale for photonic Gaussian boson sampling architectures tied to recent average-case hardness results.
main_result: Random hypercube linear optics generate broadly near-maximal averaged subsystem entanglement at logarithmic circuit depth.
application_angle: It clarifies how shallow a photonic network can be while still producing entanglement structure relevant to scalable sampling advantage.

title: Benchmarking the computational power of quantum computers
abstract: Quantum computing hardware is advancing rapidly toward utility-scale machines that will enable scientific breakthroughs. Many teams are pursuing distinct and difficult-to-compare routes to this goal, using different qubit technologies and logical architectures. Tracking progress toward quantum utility therefore requires rigorous benchmarks that measure computational capability relative to utility-scale challenge problems and enable fair comparison across disparate platforms. Here we demonstrate direct, cross-platform measurement of quantum computational capability using a new benchmark that quantifies the size of the largest computationally relevant quantum circuits that a machine can execute successfully and the speed at which it can execute them. We apply this quantum universal operation performance system (QUOPS) experimentally to leading processors from Quantinuum, Google, and IBM, computing directly on physical qubits. Translating state-of-the-art resource requirements for recognized challenge problems that represent useful quantum computation into effective QUOPS circuit sizes shows that computational capability must grow by 5 orders of magnitude, motivating fault-tolerant approaches. We use the same benchmark to assess the performance of a simple fault-tolerant logical-qubit processor implemented on up to eight [[7,1,3]]-encoded logical qubits using Quantinuum Helios-1, and project the growth of capability across successive generations of fault-tolerant quantum computers to show how QUOPS can track progress toward quantum scientific utility.
one_liner: Introduces QUOPS, a cross-platform benchmark for quantum computational capability, and applies it to Quantinuum, Google, and IBM processors.
why_it_matters: Gives a hardware-agnostic way to compare useful circuit execution capacity and quantify the remaining gap to utility-scale quantum computing.
detailed_summary: The authors define a quantum universal operation performance system benchmark that measures the largest computationally relevant circuits a machine can execute successfully and how fast it executes them. They experimentally apply it to physical-qubit processors from Quantinuum, Google, and IBM, then compare observed capability to resource requirements for useful quantum challenge problems. The work also evaluates a small fault-tolerant logical-qubit processor on Quantinuum Helios-1 using up to eight [[7,1,3]] encoded logical qubits.
main_result: QUOPS experimentally quantifies current computational capability and indicates roughly five orders of magnitude growth is still needed for selected utility-scale workloads.
application_angle: The benchmark can guide procurement, roadmap tracking, and fair comparison across qubit technologies and logical architectures.

title: Parallel Circuit Execution for Scalable Quantum Computation
abstract: Today's quantum processors have tens to hundreds of physical qubits, but reliable execution of arbitrary circuits remains limited to fewer than 30 entangled qubits across hardware modalities. Building upon prior work, we introduce an error- and topology-aware method for mapping multiple independent circuits onto disjoint regions of a single large-scale QPU for parallel circuit execution. For applications with many similarly sized circuits, such as observable estimation for Hamiltonian simulation, this approach can reduce billed QPU execution time, with ideal speedup proportional to the number of usable partitions. We demonstrate the approach on IBM's 156-qubit ibm_boston processor using standard QED-C benchmark and Hamiltonian-based observable-estimation workloads. Compared with standard sequential execution, parallel execution reduces billed execution time by 3.5-5.5x while retaining 83-92% of the sequential fidelity. We further evaluate the scaling of parallel circuit execution using GPU-accelerated classical simulation, distributing measurement circuits across GPUs via MPI. Using CUDA-Q on the NERSC Perlmutter system, we achieve up to 13.8x speedup on 16 GPUs (86% parallel efficiency) for an H2 electronic-structure simulation, with scaling evaluated across multiple Hamiltonians and circuit counts. These results provide an indication of the performance ceiling that parallel execution on future quantum hardware may eventually approach. Both execution modes are implemented as a runtime option within the QED-C Application-Oriented Benchmark suite. Together, the results show that circuit-level parallelism can reduce execution cost on current quantum hardware and simulation time on GPU clusters, with the potential for greater benefits as device quality and qubit counts increase.
one_liner: Demonstrates topology- and error-aware parallel execution of independent quantum circuits on one QPU, cutting billed runtime on IBM hardware.
why_it_matters: Shows a practical route to higher throughput and lower cost for workloads made of many modest-size circuits, such as observable estimation.
detailed_summary: The paper maps multiple independent circuits onto disjoint regions of a large quantum processor using device topology and error information. On IBM's 156-qubit ibm_boston processor, QED-C and Hamiltonian observable-estimation workloads see 3.5-5.5x reductions in billed execution time while retaining 83-92% of sequential fidelity. GPU-accelerated CUDA-Q simulations on NERSC Perlmutter show up to 13.8x speedup on 16 GPUs for an H2 electronic-structure workload.
platform_or_system: partitioned superconducting QPU and GPU simulator
main_result: Parallel circuit execution reduces billed QPU time by 3.5-5.5x on IBM hardware with moderate fidelity loss.
application_angle: This can immediately improve throughput for variational, benchmarking, and Hamiltonian-estimation workloads composed of many independent circuits.

title: Sparse-Blossom Decoding in $o(1)$ Time
abstract: Matching-based decoding is widely used in quantum error correction, and accelerating it is key to enabling fast and scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation. Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoding provides rigorous guarantees for error suppression, while sparse blossom enables its practical implementation at modest problem sizes. However, the runtime of existing sparse-blossom implementations unavoidably increases with problem size, motivating a rigorous parallelization framework that guarantees correctness and a runtime shorter than the syndrome-extraction timescale. Here, we present such a framework and prove that the resulting parallel sparse-blossom algorithm produces the same correction as the original, non-parallel sparse blossom. For the rotated surface code with code distance $d$ and physical error rates below a finite threshold, we prove that the average parallel runtime of decoding for $O(d)$ rounds of syndrome extraction is upper bounded by a quasi-polylogarithmic function of $d$. For a $d$-round decoding window, this implies that the average parallel runtime per round is $o(1)$. We also perform numerical simulation to identify conditions under which the parallel runtime per round decreases with increasing code distance. These results suggest that increasing code distance need not lead to longer parallel decoding times, providing a foundation for scalable parallel matching-based decoding.
one_liner: Presents a correctness-preserving parallel sparse-blossom decoder whose average per-round runtime can shrink with surface-code distance.
why_it_matters: Fast, scalable decoding is a central hardware bottleneck for fault-tolerant quantum computing, especially under real-time syndrome extraction.
detailed_summary: The work develops a rigorous parallelization framework for sparse-blossom minimum-weight perfect matching decoding and proves it returns the same correction as the serial algorithm. For rotated surface codes below threshold, the average parallel runtime over O(d) syndrome rounds is bounded by a quasi-polylogarithmic function of code distance d. For a d-round window, this implies o(1) average parallel runtime per round, supported by numerical studies identifying decreasing-runtime regimes.
main_result: Parallel sparse-blossom decoding is proven correction-equivalent to serial sparse blossom while achieving subconstant average per-round runtime scaling in the stated regime.
application_angle: It supports real-time decoding architectures where increasing code distance does not necessarily increase decoding latency.

title: Resonance-Enhanced Time Reflection at Photonic Temporal Interfaces
abstract: Photonic temporal interfaces enable dynamic control of light fields, yet strong time reflection at optical frequencies remains challenging because conventional approaches demand large material refractive-index changes on ultrafast timescales. Here, we introduce a resonance-assisted mechanism that harnesses both polarization energy accumulated in a dispersive medium prior to the temporal interface and strongly increased energy supplied by the modulation system. We show that, under a specific critical condition, rapidly increasing the material resonance frequency yields orders-of-magnitude stronger time-reflected power flux density than what conventional plasma-frequency modulation provides. To implement this mechanism in optical systems, we identify two routes based on dielectric and plasmonic structural resonances. For the plasmonic route, we develop an analytical effective-medium model of conducting-oxide cylinder arrays, in which localized surface-plasmon resonances transform the constituent Drude response into a geometrically tunable effective Lorentz response. Using cadmium oxide as a representative material, we predict an enhancement exceeding three orders of magnitude in the summed reflected-mode power coefficient relative to the same homogeneous material under the same modest plasma-frequency modulation, even in the presence of realistic losses. These findings establish spatial resonance engineering as an effective route to strong temporal scattering with reduced demands on intrinsic material tunability.
one_liner: Proposes resonance-enhanced temporal interfaces that can boost optical time-reflected power by orders of magnitude under modest modulation.
why_it_matters: Offers a route to strong temporal scattering at optical frequencies without requiring unrealistically large ultrafast refractive-index changes.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces a resonance-assisted mechanism that uses polarization energy stored in a dispersive medium plus energy supplied by rapid modulation to enhance time reflection. It identifies a critical condition where increasing the material resonance frequency gives much stronger reflected power than conventional plasma-frequency modulation. For cadmium-oxide conducting-oxide cylinder arrays, an effective-medium model predicts more than three orders of magnitude enhancement in summed reflected-mode power even with realistic losses.
main_result: Spatial resonance engineering is predicted to enhance optical time-reflected power by over three orders of magnitude compared with homogeneous-material modulation.
application_angle: The mechanism could enable practical temporal photonic devices for frequency conversion, nonreciprocal wave control, and dynamic light manipulation.

title: Revealing Hidden Inversion Symmetry Breaking in ZrTe$_5$ via Phonon-Assisted Heterodyne Amplification
abstract: ZrTe$_5$ is a sensitive topological material where small perturbations can alter its electronic structure. Its equilibrium crystal structure has been widely regarded as centrosymmetric, while recent experiments have raised the possibility of inversion-symmetry breaking. Here we probe this hidden symmetry lowering using nonlinear optical spectroscopy. Although conventional second-harmonic generation does not resolve an equilibrium symmetry-breaking signal, terahertz-field-induced second-harmonic generation (TFISH) reveals it through phonon-assisted heterodyne amplification. A coherently driven infrared-active phonon acts as a local oscillator for the vanishingly weak second-order susceptibility $χ^{(2)}$, converting an otherwise undetectable symmetry-breaking response into a phonon-frequency modulation of the TFISH signal. The field-linear scaling of this modulation demonstrates $χ^{(2)}$ is an equilibrium susceptibility rather than a response induced by the THz field. Polarization- and temperature-dependent measurements identify a bulk polar distortion along the crystallographic $a$ axis that persists to room temperature, while the $c$ axis remains nonpolar. These results provide direct optical evidence for equilibrium inversion-symmetry breaking in bulk ZrTe$_5$ and establish a structural constraint for understanding its electronic and topological properties.
one_liner: Uses phonon-assisted TFISH to reveal weak equilibrium inversion-symmetry breaking in bulk ZrTe5 up to room temperature.
why_it_matters: Provides a sensitive nonlinear-optical probe of hidden symmetry lowering in a topological material where small structural changes reshape electronic behavior.
detailed_summary: The authors use terahertz-field-induced second-harmonic generation to detect an equilibrium chi(2) response that conventional SHG cannot resolve. A coherently driven infrared-active phonon acts as a local oscillator, heterodyne-amplifying the weak symmetry-breaking signal as a phonon-frequency modulation. Field-linear scaling, polarization dependence, and temperature scans indicate a bulk polar distortion along the crystallographic a axis that persists to room temperature.
main_result: Phonon-assisted heterodyne amplification reveals bulk equilibrium inversion-symmetry breaking in ZrTe5, with a polar a-axis distortion persisting to room temperature.
application_angle: The method can sensitively diagnose weak polar order and symmetry constraints relevant to topological-material devices and ultrafast optical characterization.

title: Quantum neural network equipped with backpropagation on a qudit processor
abstract: Quantum neural networks (QNNs), one of the fundamental algorithms in quantum machine learning, have been widely used in classification and identification tasks. However, the capabilities of QNNs are constrained by their size, which is determined by the dimension of the Hilbert space of the underlying quantum processor. Multi-level quantum digits (qudits) offer access to a higher-dimensional Hilbert space compared to two-level qubits, enabling the construction of more expressive QNNs. In this work, we report an experimental demonstration of qudit-based QNN using a trapped $\rm ^{40}Ca^+$ ion. We train the QNN using a hybrid quantum-classical implementation of backpropagation and achieve an experimental classification accuracy of $95.7\%$ on a test image set. This demonstration highlights the potential of qudit-based processors to QNN architectures and provides a framework for implementing qudit-based QNNs across various quantum devices.
one_liner: Demonstrates a backpropagation-trained qudit quantum neural network on a single trapped calcium ion.
why_it_matters: Using ion qudits expands Hilbert-space capacity without adding more physical particles, a practical route for compact quantum processors.
detailed_summary: The experiment implements a quantum neural network on a trapped 40Ca+ ion operated as a multi-level qudit rather than a two-level qubit. Training uses a hybrid quantum-classical backpropagation procedure, and the device reaches 95.7% classification accuracy on a test image set. The work is notable because it demonstrates algorithmic learning functionality directly on a higher-dimensional quantum processor.
main_result: A qudit-based QNN trained by hybrid backpropagation achieved 95.7% experimental test-set classification accuracy.
application_angle: The approach could make small quantum processors more expressive for machine-learning workloads by exploiting internal levels instead of scaling qubit count.

title: Security Implications of Measurement Based Crosstalk on Superconducting Quantum Computers
abstract: Crosstalk is one of the major issues for scalability of superconducting quantum processors. But it can also be used by threat actors to intentionally sabotage computations and steal information. This paper analyzes data leakage due to crosstalk during qubit measurement. Prior research yielded an accuracy of 96% in classifying measurement of one qubit in IBM quantum computers. When evaluated on superconducting hardware from VTT, we achieved an accuracy of 71.68% with similar framework. Our extended framework with additional labels yields an accuracy of 76.30% for classifying measurement of one qubit and 53.37% for measurement of two qubits using Support Vector Machine (SVM). Experimental results indicate that measurement operation on a qubit can affect the probability of measuring adjacent qubits. The impact on the target qubit is dependent on the number of neighboring qubits measured and also the measurement outcome.
one_liner: Measures how superconducting-qubit readout crosstalk can leak information and enable computation sabotage.
why_it_matters: It reframes hardware crosstalk as a security channel, relevant for shared cloud quantum processors and trustworthy execution.
detailed_summary: The paper studies measurement-induced crosstalk on superconducting quantum hardware and evaluates whether adjacent-qubit readout signatures reveal private measurement activity. On VTT hardware, a prior-style classifier reaches 71.68% accuracy, while an extended SVM framework reaches 76.30% for one-qubit measurement classification and 53.37% for two-qubit cases. The results show that both the number of measured neighbors and their outcomes affect target-qubit statistics.
main_result: Measurement operations on neighboring qubits were classified above chance from crosstalk signatures, demonstrating a practical leakage channel.
application_angle: The findings motivate crosstalk-aware isolation, scheduling, and security testing for multi-user superconducting quantum computers.

title: Factoring six-digit integers with superconducting quantum circuits
abstract: Integer factorization is a central computational problem with important applications in public-key cryptography. Here, we demonstrate a quantum factorization protocol using a superconducting circuit. Microwave drives are used to engineer a highly tunable effective two-level Hamiltonian whose eigenvalues can be measured spectroscopically. The target integer \(N\) and each candidate factor pair (\(p\),\(q\)) are encoded into the amplitudes, frequencies, and phases of the applied microwave fields. By scanning the candidate pairs while monitoring the spectral response at zero energy, we identify the factor pairs of integers up to six digits. The protocol requires neither two-qubit gates nor quantum entanglement. Its performance is currently limited by the precision of microwave control and the finite linewidth of the spectroscopic response. Improved control accuracy and longer coherence times would extend the accessible range of integers.
one_liner: Uses a driven superconducting circuit to spectroscopically identify factor pairs of integers up to six digits.
why_it_matters: Although not Shor-style scalable factoring, it is a hardware demonstration of analog Hamiltonian encoding for arithmetic search.
detailed_summary: The experiment engineers an effective tunable two-level Hamiltonian in a superconducting circuit using microwave drives. The integer and candidate factor pairs are encoded into drive amplitudes, frequencies, and phases, then scanned while monitoring spectral response at zero energy. The method identifies factor pairs for integers up to six digits without two-qubit gates or entanglement, with present limits set by microwave precision and linewidth.
main_result: The system experimentally factored integers up to six digits by detecting zero-energy spectral responses for correct candidate pairs.
application_angle: It illustrates how precision-controlled superconducting hardware can implement specialized analog search protocols, even outside gate-model algorithms.

title: Violating a Bell Inequality: What to Do When You Lose Your Quantum System
abstract: The detection loophole is a well-known loophole in Bell nonlocality motivated by the inefficiency of detectors used in Bell experiments. However, this inefficiency is actually a ubiquitous feature of any photonic platform for quantum networks since photons are readily absorbed by the surrounding environment. When the quantum system, usually a photon, is lost, what should the parties output? The most natural choice is to fall back to a deterministic strategy where each party produces an output via a function of her local input. In this paper, we study how to choose such a fallback strategy for general Bell inequalities with respect to different efficiencies $η$ to maximize the possible violation. We mathematically prove that for the CHSH inequality, there exists a fallback strategy that is optimal for all $η$. However, in general, we find that the optimal fallback strategy can vary with $η$, sometimes in surprising ways. For example, we find an example of a Bell inequality where the optimal fallback strategy near the threshold efficiency is not an optimal deterministic strategy in the lossless setting. Our results can reduce the efficiency requirements for closing the detection loophole and thus are useful for applications of Bell inequality violation, such as quantum telepathy or device-independent quantum key distribution.
one_liner: Optimizes deterministic fallback outputs for lossy photonic Bell tests and device-independent protocols.
why_it_matters: Better fallback strategies can lower efficiency requirements for loophole-resistant Bell violations in quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The work asks what parties should output when a photon is lost in a Bell experiment, treating loss as a central feature of photonic quantum networking. It proves that for CHSH there is a fallback strategy optimal for all efficiencies, while for general Bell inequalities the optimal deterministic fallback can depend on efficiency. The analysis identifies cases where the near-threshold strategy is not the lossless-optimal deterministic strategy.
main_result: The paper derives efficiency-dependent fallback strategies that can improve Bell-violation robustness under photon loss.
application_angle: This is directly relevant to device-independent QKD and other quantum-network protocols where detector inefficiency and channel loss are unavoidable.

title: Travelling Dark State Polariton as a Viable Quantum Memory in a Solid-State Medium
abstract: We theorize a quantum memory based on the dark-state polariton field, formed by the superposition of atomic and photonic states of a travelling probe laser pulse under the application of standing wave modes of a dominant control laser pulse using a lambda-level scheme Electromagnetically Induced Transparency in a solid medium. We show how an enhancement in the storage time for the pulse is achieved by eliminating pulse broadening due to diffusion. At last, we propose an experiment that can help realize the storage of a probe pulse in the hyperfine levels $^3\text{H}_4 \leftrightarrow ^1\text{D}_2$ of $\text{Pr}^{3+}:\text{Y}_2\text{SiO}_5$, cryogenically cooled at $4.5\text{ K}$. We also discuss multiple applications the storage of the quantum states the probe pulse with a prolonged time interval must have.
one_liner: Proposes a solid-state travelling dark-state polariton quantum memory using EIT in Pr3+:Y2SiO5.
why_it_matters: Solid-state optical memories with longer storage times are enabling components for repeaters and synchronized quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a theoretical quantum memory based on a travelling probe pulse converted into a dark-state polariton under standing-wave control fields in a lambda-level EIT scheme. The design targets reduced pulse broadening from diffusion to extend storage time. A proposed implementation uses the hyperfine levels of cryogenic Pr3+:Y2SiO5 at 4.5 K.
main_result: The authors propose a diffusion-suppressed travelling dark-state polariton memory architecture for prolonged probe-pulse storage.
application_angle: Such a memory could support buffering, synchronization, and state storage in solid-state quantum communication nodes.

title: Design and Finite-Element Analysis of a New Inclined Blade-Electrode Architecture for Trapped-Ion Quantum Information Processing
abstract: The development of scalable quantum technologies requires ion-trap architectures that provide strong and stable confinement while minimizing motional heating caused by electric-field noise. Trapped-ion systems offer long coherence times and high-fidelity quantum control; however, anomalous motional heating from electrode surfaces can limit their performance. This study presents a finite-element analysis of a novel inclined ion-trap architecture, focusing on the effects of electrode geometry and blade separation on confinement strength, secular frequencies, motional heating, thermal response, and RF stability. Five trap inclinations were investigated using three-dimensional electrostatic simulations for blade separations of 5 to 35 um. The RF electric-field distribution was used to determine the effective pseudopotential, trap depth, secular frequencies, and normal modes. An empirical electric-field-noise model was then used to estimate the motional heating rate for frequency-noise exponents alpha = 3, 3.5, and 4. The results reveal a trade-off between confinement strength and ion-electrode distance. Blade separations of approximately 25 to 35 um provide a favorable design regime. At 25 um, the predicted heating rate is approximately 127 to 135 quanta per second for alpha = 3, but the RF stability margin is lower (qmax approximately 1.9). At 35 um, the stability is substantially improved (qmax approximately 0.52), while the heating rate increases to approximately 1570 to 1820 quanta per second. These results provide design guidelines for optimizing inclined ion traps for future trapped-ion quantum-information architectures.
one_liner: Finite-element study maps confinement, heating, and RF stability trade-offs in inclined blade-electrode ion traps.
why_it_matters: Quantitative geometry guidance helps design ion traps that balance strong confinement against surface-noise-induced motional heating.
detailed_summary: The study simulates a new inclined blade-electrode trap architecture using three-dimensional electrostatic finite-element analysis. It evaluates blade separations from 5 to 35 um and multiple inclinations, extracting pseudopotential, trap depth, secular frequencies, normal modes, thermal response, and RF stability. The results identify 25 to 35 um separations as a favorable design regime, with explicit trade-offs between heating rate and stability margin.
main_result: The analysis predicts practical operating regimes, including low heating near 25 um and improved RF stability near 35 um blade separation.
application_angle: The design rules can inform scalable trapped-ion processors and precision ion-based sensing platforms where heating and stability are limiting factors.

title: Interplay between growth conditions and formation of localized light emitters in epitaxial AlN thin films
abstract: AlN is a promising material for integrated quantum photonics due to its broad transparency window, its compatibility with CMOS technology, and the possibility to host localized light emitters acting as single photon sources. However, little is understood yet about the microscopic nature and formation mechanisms of these light emitters. In this contribution, we demonstrate that their formation efficiency depends significantly on the growth conditions of the AlN thin film. We reveal that localized light emitters with distinct zero-phonon lines in the 600--800~nm range can be efficiently formed in epitaxial AlN thin films grown under N-rich conditions by exposing the AlN to a post-growth treatment consisting in a proton irradiation followed by an annealing process. In contrast, the density of light emitters formed in AlN grown under Al-rich conditions remains low, even after the thin films have been exposed to the post-growth treatment. These results open a pathway toward a better understanding of the microscopic nature of these light emission centers, as well as their engineered integration as quantum light sources in AlN-based optomechanical platforms.
one_liner: Growth stoichiometry strongly controls proton-irradiation activation of visible localized emitters in epitaxial AlN films.
why_it_matters: It gives a materials knob for engineering AlN single-photon emitters compatible with integrated photonic and optomechanical platforms.
detailed_summary: The work studies localized light emitters in epitaxial AlN thin films after proton irradiation and annealing. N-rich growth produces efficient formation of emitters with zero-phonon lines in the 600-800 nm range, while Al-rich growth yields much lower emitter density under the same treatment. The result links emitter activation to growth conditions, narrowing the search for microscopic defect origins.
main_result: N-rich epitaxial AlN enables efficient formation of visible localized emitters after proton irradiation and annealing.
application_angle: Controlled emitter creation is a practical step toward integrated AlN quantum light sources on CMOS-compatible photonic chips.

title: Average-case hardness of Betti number estimation
abstract: We establish the average-case hardness of Betti number estimation on random clique complexes via a reduction from the planted clique problem. We further show that our reduction implies a series of hardness results for many problems in both classical and quantum Topological Data Analysis (qTDA). Under the classical planted clique conjecture, no randomized polynomial-time Betti number estimator achieves additive error below $\tfrac12$ with constant advantage. Under a new quantum planted clique conjecture that we introduce, the same conclusion holds for quantum polynomial-time algorithms. We also obtain related conditional hardness results for homology vanishing, additive approximations with larger error tolerances, preparation of simplex and harmonic states, cycle recovery, and counting eigenvalues at low energy. Our reduction clarifies the structural requirements for quantum advantage in TDA and provides a new lens to investigate the classical and quantum complexity of related problems.
one_liner: The paper proves conditional average-case hardness for Betti-number estimation on random clique complexes.
why_it_matters: It clarifies where quantum topological data analysis may or may not deliver practical quantum advantage.
detailed_summary: The authors reduce planted clique to Betti-number estimation on random clique complexes. Under classical and proposed quantum planted-clique conjectures, polynomial-time classical and quantum estimators cannot achieve additive error below 1/2 with constant advantage. The analysis also extends to homology vanishing, simplex and harmonic state preparation, cycle recovery, and low-energy eigenvalue counting.
main_result: The paper establishes conditional average-case hardness barriers for a family of classical and quantum TDA tasks.
application_angle: For application-oriented quantum algorithms, it helps identify which TDA workloads are unlikely to yield easy practical speedups.

title: Spatial symmetry in few-photon interference and quantum metrology
abstract: In previous work [Physical Review Letters, 136(6):060807, 2026], we developed a symmetry-based framework for generalized Hong-Ou-Mandel interference and its applications to quantum metrology. Here, we apply this framework to experimentally accessible configurations involving a few photons and explore how it sheds new light on a variety of existing results while suggesting new experimental perspectives. We first reinterpret a two-photon Mach-Zehnder interferometer as a generalized Hong-Ou-Mandel experiment and show how its photon-counting statistics and metrological performance follow from the spatial symmetry of an effective probe state. We then study two coherently pumped parametric photon-pair sources, derive their complete output distribution, and connect source indistinguishability with spatial symmetry. Finally, we extend the discussion to a three-mode interferometer and show that the same symmetry principles provide a natural description of three-photon interference in tritter configurations.
one_liner: Few-photon interferometers are recast through spatial symmetry to unify interference statistics and metrological performance.
why_it_matters: The framework can guide experimentally accessible photon-counting metrology with Mach-Zehnder, pair-source, and tritter setups.
detailed_summary: This paper applies a symmetry-based generalized Hong-Ou-Mandel framework to few-photon interferometry. It interprets two-photon Mach-Zehnder statistics and metrological sensitivity through the spatial symmetry of an effective probe state. It further analyzes coherently pumped parametric pair sources and three-photon tritter interference, connecting indistinguishability and output distributions to symmetry classes.
main_result: Spatial symmetry provides a unified description of photon-counting statistics and metrological behavior in several few-photon interferometers.
application_angle: The results suggest cleaner design rules for photonic sensing experiments that exploit multiphoton interference.

title: Fast quantum squeezing of a nanomechanical oscillator with an inverted potential
abstract: Nonclassical states of nano- and micro-mechanical motion enable measurements beyond the standard quantum limit and constitute a key resource for quantum sensing and metrology. The most strongly squeezed mechanical states to date have been generated with electromechanical platforms under cryogenic refrigeration and using reservoir engineering. To push mechanical systems deeper into the quantum-squeezed regime requires protocols that increase the rate at which squeezing is generated to more strongly overcome the decoherence rate at which state purity is lost. Here, we squeeze the 800 kHz libration mode of a silica nanoparticle optically levitated in vacuum at room temperature. We expose our mechanical oscillator to an optically generated inverted potential, where the squeezing operation proceeds at an exponentially accelerated rate. We reach a squeezed quadrature variance 11 dB below the vacuum fluctuations within 250 ns. Our protocol establishes a new paradigm for generating quantum squeezing of mechanical motion and offers a platform for quantum-enhanced sensing with massive oscillators.
one_liner: A levitated silica nanoparticle is squeezed 11 dB below vacuum noise in 250 ns using an optically generated inverted potential.
why_it_matters: Fast room-temperature mechanical squeezing could enable quantum-enhanced sensing before decoherence erases nonclassical motion.
detailed_summary: The experiment squeezes the 800 kHz libration mode of an optically levitated silica nanoparticle in vacuum at room temperature. By applying an optically generated inverted potential, the squeezing rate is exponentially accelerated relative to conventional protocols. The reported squeezed quadrature variance reaches 11 dB below vacuum fluctuations within 250 ns.
main_result: The authors demonstrate 11 dB mechanical quadrature squeezing in 250 ns at room temperature.
application_angle: Rapid preparation of nonclassical massive motion is directly relevant to force sensing, inertial sensing, and tests of macroscopic quantum mechanics.

title: Grover Search with Semiconductor Spin Qubits at Ambient Conditions
abstract: Grover's algorithm is executed on a commercial quantum computer based on nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond operating under ambient conditions, achieving fidelities up to $99.98\,\%$. Within a $N=8$ search space of three solid-state nuclear spin qubits, the measured success probabilities of finding a single or two marked states are $(77.3 \pm 3.4)\,\%$ and $(87.0 \pm 4.2)\,\%$, respectively. These values surpass published results for superconducting qubits or any quantum computer operating at room temperature. In addition, the paper also details the calibrated fidelities of the implemented universal gate set.
one_liner: Grover search is run on room-temperature NV-center spin qubits with up to 99.98% calibrated fidelities.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates a small algorithm on commercial solid-state quantum hardware operating under ambient conditions.
detailed_summary: The paper reports Grover's algorithm on a commercial nitrogen-vacancy diamond quantum computer operating at ambient conditions. In a three-qubit N=8 search space using solid-state nuclear spin qubits, the measured success probabilities are 77.3% for one marked state and 87.0% for two marked states. The authors also report calibrated fidelities for the implemented universal gate set, with values up to 99.98%.
main_result: A room-temperature NV-based processor executes three-qubit Grover search with reported success probabilities above comparable published room-temperature results.
application_angle: Ambient-operation spin processors could reduce infrastructure barriers for deployable quantum computing and education-scale quantum hardware.

title: Unified scaling of transmon sub-resonant parametric drive strength limits
abstract: Achieving fast gates and high-fidelity readout in superconducting quantum circuits often benefits from the use of large amplitude microwave drives. As the strength increases, unwanted effects such as excitation out of the logical states also become more prevalent. In transmon qubits, coherent controls relying on sub-resonant drives are fundamentally limited by the eventual appearance of strong hybridization in the spectrum. Understanding how this threshold depends on intrinsic device parameters is vital for the design and operation of circuits utilizing the transmon as a source of nonlinearity. In this work, we present an experimental study of 14 transmons with a wide range of anharmonicities, and use comparison with Floquet branch analysis and semiclassical simulations to establish a straightforward relationship between the critical value of the effective drive amplitude $η_{\max}$ and the ratio $γ=ω_q/α$, where $ω_q$ is the transmon frequency and $-α$ is the anharmonicity. For the case where the transmon is used as a parametrically driven coupler, these results further allow us to estimate maximum parametric interaction rates, which informs the circuit design process for optimizing gate rates and fidelities.
one_liner: Measurements on 14 transmons reveal a scaling law for sub-resonant parametric drive strength limits.
why_it_matters: The result gives circuit designers a practical bound for faster gates and parametric couplers before leakage and hybridization dominate.
detailed_summary: The study experimentally probes 14 transmons spanning a range of anharmonicities under strong sub-resonant microwave drives. Comparing data with Floquet branch analysis and semiclassical simulations, it relates the critical effective drive amplitude to gamma = omega_q/alpha. For parametrically driven couplers, this scaling can be translated into estimates of maximum achievable interaction rates.
main_result: The authors establish a simple empirical and theoretical scaling for the maximum usable sub-resonant parametric drive amplitude in transmons.
application_angle: This helps optimize superconducting-qubit gate speed and readout/coupler performance while avoiding drive-induced leakage and spectral hybridization.

title: Momentum microscopy of ultrafast electron emission from a strongly driven optical nanoantenna
abstract: Metallic nanostructures in combination with femtosecond lasers are a well-suited platform for the control of photoelectrons by strong and nano-localized driving fields, with high relevance for ultrafast, coherent electron emitters and petahertz electronics. Photoelectron spectroscopy resolves such photoelectron dynamics, but lacks nanoscale spatial resolution, making it only suited for single emitters or homogeneous arrays. We report the first strong-field experiment combining both photoemission electron microscopy and momentum microscopy, two complementary techniques providing spatial and momentum resolution within the same instrument. We apply this new methodology to a double-hole nanoantenna with sub-10 nm apex radii, demonstrating the potential of this approach for the control of photoelectrons in heterogeneous nanostructured samples using few-cycle light fields. Our measurements reveal distinct signatures of two classes of electron trajectories in the near-field. Quiver trajectories result in directed, angularly more focused emission, whereas subcycle trajectories give rise to a broader transverse momentum distribution. Surprisingly, this observation disagrees with previously reported emission characteristics from nanotip emitters, which we classify as a special case of a broader class of curved emitter surfaces driven by ultrashort light fields. This demonstrates both the impact of sophisticated electron detection methods and the potential of strong-field control of electrons in nanoscale geometries.
one_liner: Combines PEEM and momentum microscopy to map strong-field electron emission from a femtosecond-driven optical nanoantenna.
why_it_matters: Spatial and momentum-resolved emission diagnostics can guide nanoscale coherent electron sources and petahertz optoelectronic devices.
detailed_summary: The work reports a strong-field experiment that combines photoemission electron microscopy with momentum microscopy in one instrument. Applied to a double-hole metallic nanoantenna with sub-10 nm apex radii, it resolves both where and with what transverse momentum electrons are emitted under few-cycle optical driving. The data distinguish quiver trajectories, which produce more directed angular emission, from subcycle trajectories with broader transverse momentum spread.
main_result: The authors demonstrate simultaneous spatial and momentum microscopy of ultrafast strong-field photoemission from a heterogeneous optical nanoantenna.
application_angle: The method provides a practical diagnostic for engineering coherent nanoscale electron emitters and ultrafast lightwave electronics.

title: Error Correction in a Distributed Quantum Computer
abstract: Building fault-tolerant quantum computers with large numbers of logical qubits requires both scalable hardware architectures and error-correcting codes that make efficient use of physical qubits. Photonic interconnects address both of these challenges by allowing the physical qubits to be distributed across multiple processors while providing the non-local connectivity necessary to implement resource-efficient codes such as high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. A key requirement for realising this architecture is the ability to perform stabiliser measurements between remote processors, which has not previously been demonstrated experimentally. Here we report the first experimental demonstration of distributed quantum error detection and correction. We generate entanglement between network qubits in two separate trapped-ion processors and use it to perform remote syndrome measurements on data qubits. We first realise a distributed [[2, 1, 1]] repetition code, detecting phase-flip errors on a logical qubit encoded across the two modules in real time and suppressing logical errors. We then combine these mid-circuit syndrome measurements with real-time feedforward to actively correct arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state. These results provide an experimental foundation for quantum error correction (QEC) across modular quantum architectures.
one_liner: Demonstrates remote syndrome measurements and active error correction across two trapped-ion quantum processors.
why_it_matters: It is a key experimental step toward modular fault-tolerant machines using photonic links and high-connectivity codes.
detailed_summary: The paper demonstrates distributed quantum error detection and correction using entanglement between network qubits in two separated trapped-ion processors. The experiment realizes a distributed [[2,1,1]] repetition code that detects phase-flip errors on a logical qubit encoded across modules. It further combines mid-circuit remote syndrome measurements with real-time feedforward to correct arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state.
main_result: The authors experimentally perform stabilizer measurements between remote processors and use them for distributed error detection and correction.
application_angle: This validates a core primitive for scalable modular quantum computers connected by photonic interconnects.

title: Exact Fock Amplitudes of the Cubic-Phase Gate on Arbitrary Pure Gaussian States
abstract: The cubic phase gate is the only non-Gaussian element of universal continuous-variable quantum computation. Its Fock amplitudes are known in closed form only when the input is a Fock state. For a Gaussian input the usual route is to build the cubic quadrature in a truncated Fock space and exponentiate it, which alters the generator before the exponential is taken. A closed form is obtained here for every pure single-mode Gaussian input, with the squeezing along any quadrature axis and with arbitrary displacement and boost. It is a finite combination of the Airy function and its derivative, and the argument is shared by all Fock indices, so a whole Fock profile costs two Airy evaluations. A recurrence is also derived that builds each coefficient from the four preceding ones, together with the regime in which it is stable. Evaluating the closed form at the weak nonlinearities of current experiments requires care, since its terms grow large and alternate in sign. The precision this demands is quantified, and the truncated construction is benchmarked against the exact result, whose error at cutoffs in common use is found to be of the same size as the quantity being computed.
one_liner: Derives exact Fock amplitudes for applying the cubic-phase gate to arbitrary pure single-mode Gaussian states.
why_it_matters: Accurate non-Gaussian gate modeling is crucial for continuous-variable quantum computing and photonic state engineering.
detailed_summary: The paper gives a closed-form expression for the Fock amplitudes produced by a cubic-phase gate acting on arbitrary pure single-mode Gaussian inputs with general squeezing and displacement. The formula uses a finite combination of the Airy function and its derivative, with a shared argument across Fock indices, plus a recurrence relation for efficient profile generation. It also quantifies numerical precision requirements at weak nonlinearities and shows that common truncated-generator methods can have errors comparable to the computed amplitudes.
main_result: The authors obtain exact, efficiently evaluable Fock coefficients for cubic-phase-gated pure Gaussian inputs and benchmark truncation errors.
application_angle: The result improves simulation, calibration, and verification of experimentally realistic continuous-variable non-Gaussian gates.

title: Experimental observation of exceptional bound states in the continuum
abstract: We experimentally demonstrate second- and third-order exceptional bound states in the continuum (EP-BICs), formed by the merging of two and three symmetry-protected BICs at an exceptional point (EP). Our passive reciprocal acoustic platform consists of symmetry-protected BIC cavities coupled through an acoustic waveguide and enables independent control of intrinsic loss, radiative loss, and near-field coupling between the cavities. A nonuniformly distributed intrinsic loss provides the non-Hermiticity required for EP formation while preserving decoupling from the waveguide radiation channel. The EP-BICs are probed using both near- and far-field excitation. In the near field, local intracavity excitation directly accesses the symmetry-protected BICs and reveals their spectral evolution. For far-field excitation, we intentionally break the protecting geometrical symmetry, converting the BICs into quasi-BICs and making them accessible through transmission measurements. Extending the system to three cavities with graded intrinsic loss realizes a third-order EP-BIC and yields a larger spectral response to the implemented coupling perturbation. These results establish a passive reciprocal route to higher-order exceptional degeneracies with independent control over intrinsic loss, near-field coupling, and radiative access.
one_liner: Experimentally realizes second- and third-order exceptional bound states in the continuum in a passive reciprocal acoustic platform.
why_it_matters: Higher-order EP-BICs offer enhanced spectral response and controllable non-Hermitian wave physics relevant to sensing and photonic analogues.
detailed_summary: The authors experimentally merge two and three symmetry-protected bound states in the continuum at exceptional points, forming second- and third-order EP-BICs. The passive reciprocal acoustic system uses BIC cavities coupled through a waveguide, with independent control of intrinsic loss, radiative loss, and near-field coupling. Near-field excitation probes the protected modes directly, while far-field transmission accesses quasi-BICs after intentional symmetry breaking; the third-order case gives a larger spectral response to coupling perturbations.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates controllable second- and third-order exceptional BICs with independently tunable loss, coupling, and radiative access.
application_angle: The platform points to passive enhanced-response sensors and transferable design rules for non-Hermitian photonic resonators.

title: Quantum Variational Approaches to Plasma Equilibrium: Cost Function Design for the Grad-Shafranov Equation
abstract: The solution of nonlinear partial differential equations constitutes an important application domain for variational quantum algorithms (VQAs). In this work, we extend the application of VQAs to plasma physics by solving the two-dimensional Grad-Shafranov equation, which describes the equilibrium state of a plasma fluid within the framework of ideal magnetohydrodynamics. For this problem, we develop and investigate two distinct cost function formulations and compare their performance in terms of solution fidelity, convergence speed and quantum resource requirements. Our results, obtained from noiseless simulations, show that the choice of cost function formulation significantly affects the performance of the variational algorithm. The Weak and Picard formulations exhibit complementary characteristics: the former consistently converges faster, whereas the latter achieves slightly lower final infidelities. Exploiting these complementary properties, we introduce a hybrid optimization strategy that combines the rapid initial convergence of the Weak formulation with the higher final accuracy of the Picard formulation. In addition, the two approaches display different quantum resource requirements due to their distinct implementations of boundary conditions. These results highlight the importance of cost function design in the development of efficient VQAs for nonlinear partial differential equations.
one_liner: Studies variational quantum algorithms for solving the Grad-Shafranov plasma equilibrium equation with different cost functions.
why_it_matters: It clarifies how cost design affects quantum PDE solvers for fusion-relevant plasma modeling, though results are simulation-only.
detailed_summary: The paper applies variational quantum algorithms to the two-dimensional nonlinear Grad-Shafranov equation from ideal magnetohydrodynamics. It compares Weak and Picard cost formulations in noiseless simulations, finding faster convergence for the Weak form and slightly lower final infidelity for the Picard form. A hybrid optimization strategy uses the Weak formulation for rapid early progress before switching to Picard for final accuracy, while also exposing different boundary-condition resource costs.
main_result: The authors show that cost-function choice strongly changes convergence, accuracy, and resource requirements for VQA solutions of the Grad-Shafranov equation.
application_angle: The study informs future quantum algorithms for fusion design workflows and physics simulation, pending hardware validation.

title: Spacetime mitigation of logical errors
abstract: Error detection can suppress noise at a lower sampling cost than probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), but leaves residual logical errors. We combine the two approaches to mitigate these errors while lowering the cost of PEC. We introduce a spacetime Pauli-Lindblad representation and use it to construct the post-selected logical noise perturbatively from physical noise and syndrome information. Individually undetected faults contribute at first order, while detected faults with canceling syndromes generate higher-order terms coupling distinct spacetime locations. To reconcile the nonlinearity of post-selection with the linearity of PEC, we formulate the combined protocol in terms of unnormalized post-selected maps, with normalization performed only after averaging. On the ibm_aachen superconducting quantum processor, Clifford experiments validate the post-selected noise model and its perturbative scaling. We then demonstrate error detection with first-order PEC for transverse-field Ising dynamics using 22 data and 27 check qubits. The combined protocol recovers the mean magnetization within statistical uncertainty through six Trotter steps and reduces the inferred sampling overhead by up to a factor of 63 relative to PEC without post-selection.
one_liner: Combines error detection with first-order probabilistic error cancellation to mitigate logical errors on an IBM superconducting processor.
why_it_matters: The protocol lowers mitigation overhead while extending useful noisy-hardware simulations with logical-error information.
detailed_summary: The work introduces a spacetime Pauli-Lindblad representation to model post-selected logical noise from physical faults and syndrome information. It formulates probabilistic error cancellation on unnormalized post-selected maps so that nonlinear post-selection can be averaged consistently. On ibm_aachen, Clifford experiments validate the perturbative noise model, and a 22-data-qubit, 27-check-qubit transverse-field Ising experiment recovers mean magnetization through six Trotter steps.
main_result: The authors demonstrate error detection plus first-order PEC on hardware, reducing inferred sampling overhead by up to 63x versus PEC without post-selection.
application_angle: This offers a practical route to deeper near-term quantum simulations by trading syndrome measurements for lower mitigation cost.

title: Effective Quantization of Lossy Nonlinear Epsilon-Near-Zero Media
abstract: In epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) materials, the vanishing real linear permittivity results in the leading-order contribution to the displacement field being nonlinear in the electric field, making conventional canonical quantization approaches highly non-trivial. Existing treatments generally quantize the linear modes first and introduce nonlinear interactions subsequently, an ordering that becomes inadequate in the ENZ regime. Here, we provide, to our knowledge, the first effective single-excitation quantization in which the near-zero linear response, leading nonlinearity, and loss jointly determine the elementary excitation. Using a solvable microscopic atomic system as a theoretical scaffold, we find that this excitation is a polariton: a dressed quasiparticle with partly field and partly material excitations whose coefficients can be parameterized by macroscopic susceptibilities. While this work considers a leading-order $χ^{(3)}$ nonlinearity, the framework could be generalized to include other nonlinear corrections, including a controllable second-order susceptibility $χ^{(2)}$ and systematic higher-order contributions $χ^{(n)}$, $n>2$. Our findings pave the way toward practical applications in quantum photonics, such as single-photon non-demolition detection, by leveraging the strong nonlinearities intrinsic to zero-index materials.
one_liner: Develops an effective single-excitation quantization for lossy nonlinear ENZ media where loss, near-zero response, and χ(3) jointly define polaritons.
why_it_matters: It gives quantum photonics a more appropriate starting point for ENZ materials, where extreme nonlinear response can enable single-photon-level devices.
detailed_summary: The paper formulates an effective quantization scheme for epsilon-near-zero media in the regime where the linear displacement response is suppressed and nonlinear terms dominate. Using a solvable microscopic atomic scaffold, it identifies the elementary excitation as a lossy nonlinear polariton with field and material components parameterized by macroscopic susceptibilities. The treatment focuses on leading χ(3) response but outlines how χ(2) and higher-order nonlinearities could enter the same framework.
main_result: The authors derive a single-excitation polariton description whose structure is set jointly by near-zero linear permittivity, χ(3) nonlinearity, and loss.
application_angle: A quantum-consistent ENZ model is a step toward designing strong-nonlinearity photonic devices such as single-photon non-demolition detectors.

title: High-rate multipartite quantum secret sharing with composable security
abstract: Future quantum communication networks will conceivably support cryptographic tasks that require entanglement among more than two users. Quantum secret sharing is a prime example where entanglement provides a direct means to coordinate untrusted parties with security from eavesdropping in a multi-party setting. However, the canonical GHZ-based protocols can be vulnerable to participant attacks, in which untrusted parties try to learn the secret without collaborating. Here, we experimentally evaluate a discrete-variable $(n,n)$-threshold quantum secret-sharing protocol whose finite-key analysis provides composable security against general attacks, including participant attacks. Using two domain-engineered entangled photon pair sources, we generate 4-qubit GHZ states at rates above $5\times10^3$ fourfold events per second and a maximum asymptotic secret key rate of $750 \pm 10$ bits per second. We then distribute the state through a 4-arm star network comprising 20km of fibre in total. From the measured event rates and error statistics, we infer that a randomised 24-hour execution with the optimised basis probability would yield a composable finite-key lower bound of 8.7 Mbits, under the assumption that the measured source and device statistics remain stationary.
one_liner: Demonstrates high-rate four-party quantum secret sharing with composable finite-key security over a 20 km fiber star network.
why_it_matters: It moves multipartite quantum cryptography from ideal GHZ demonstrations toward network-scale rates and security against participant attacks.
detailed_summary: The experiment evaluates a discrete-variable (n,n)-threshold quantum secret-sharing protocol with finite-key composable security against general and participant attacks. Two domain-engineered entangled photon-pair sources produce 4-qubit GHZ states at more than 5e3 fourfold events per second, reaching an asymptotic secret-key rate of 750 ± 10 bit/s. The authors distribute the state through a four-arm star network totaling 20 km of fiber and infer an 8.7 Mbit composable finite-key lower bound for a randomized 24 h run under stationary-device assumptions.
